title: Tony Fambro's band, its Ellington sound and Duke raiding its men
summary: Fambro's eight-piece band was called Little Duke; Sax Mallard and Nat Jones were taken by Ellington; John Levy played bass.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: When you left Stuff and went back to him, did John stay with him all that time? Was John with him then? He must have been, because you said John got you with Stuff.
Yeah. Oh, yes. Yes.
John stayed with him.
Yes. Now we're going back to Chicago now.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Yeah. Yeah, but --
Something else I'm curious about are those big bands you mentioned. You said Nat had a big band. Do you know who was in that? Can you remember?
No. I was --
You were playing --
I wasn't dry behind the ears at that time. I was just -- I was really --
Because you said you played in Hambo's band and --
[Fambro] (PHONETIC).
[Fambro] yeah, excuse me.
Yeah.
And you had the battle of the bands.
Yeah, but at that time they had stopped having those battles of the bands. I joined [Fambro] (PHONETIC) after that, but I used to be around -- hang around the bandstand to listen to them.
Oh, I see.

And they used to call [Fambro] "Little Duke", because they had some trumpet players that could growl like Cootie and you know, in those days. And it was a Duke Ellington orientated thing. But Nat Cole was a completely different thing. You know?
In what way?
The musical sound was different. It was a regular big band sound, you know?
Did Nat write for the band?
I don't know whether he wrote then or not, but I know he did a lot of writing later.
I know he did too, but I just wondered if he had then for that band.
Because he had -- he was -- he had so much taste about what he was doing musically, you know?
Uh-huh.
And -- but these -- the only thing about Tony [Fambro] -- and we had some good musicians. Oh, yeah, because two of the guys, gee whiz, Duke used to steal men out of [Fambro's] band.
Who did he steal?
One was called Sax Mallard.
Uh-huh.
He was playing alto and another one was called Nat Jones.
Uh-huh.
You know? And they were in the band. We only had those eight pieces, but you know --
What did Nat Jones play?

Nat Jones played clarinet just like Barney Bigard, and alto -- I can't describe the style. It was different, a very interesting thing. It caught Duke's ear. And he went out with Duke for a while, you know. But they didn't like that road.
Yeah, it was rough.

You know? They just didn't like that road. And they all went back -- they all went back home. They're doing well. Nat's got a lot of real estate and stuff, you know. He doesn't have to break his neck anymore. And they just play for fun, you know. Fine musicians. Just like the same situation I was speaking of -- the socio-economic thing

of Chicago. You know, the situation just sends you somewhere else, no matter what you started out to do. For survival you just have to adjust, you know. You have to keep your head above water, you know. And there's another thing, where drifting towards an Ellington type sound, because all of us admired the Ellington band. At that time, you know. We loved that band, you know? All the musicians loved it. And I think I was on my way, maybe simply because -- maybe that was one of the reasons I was with Tony [Fambro,] because -- well, it leaned towards Ellington, you know.
Do you remember who else was in the band?

Well, John Levy was playing bass in it. And then there was a fellow named Pete Smith playing drums, and the growl trumpet player's name was Russell Gillam (PHONETIC). That's the one I told you about when we were stranded, helped to do the cooking with John Levy.
Was that the Indianapolis stranding?
Yeah. There wasn't nothing but beans and rice, but it filled us up, you know. And who else? Well, Nat Jones and Sax Mallard. Until Duke started robbing Fambro of his men.
He did that to a few bands didn't he?
Yes, he did. He started robbing them. And -- but they didn't stick, you know. But --
